analysis.one_liner: Funds rental aid and affordable housing for low-income families by trimming tax breaks for wealthier households.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Major Owens with 4 Democratic cosponsors in February 1995, was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Housing Trust Fund in the Treasury and fill it with revenue raised by scaling back two tax breaks used by higher-income households: the mortgage interest and property tax deductions, for taxpayers earning over $75,000, and the tax break on inherited property, which currently lets heirs sell inherited assets without paying capital gains on the growth that happened before they inherited. That money would flow as guaranteed formula grants to cities, states, and Indian tribes to pay the gap between what low-income families can afford in rent and the market rate, and to build or rehabilitate housing that must stay affordable permanently.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families — especially extremely low-income renters paying more than half their income for housing — would gain rental assistance covering the gap between 30 percent of their income and the fair market rent, plus new permanently affordable units built or rehabilitated in their communities. Cities, states, and Indian tribes would receive dedicated, formula-based funding they could plan around, and nonprofit and for-profit housing providers would gain a new funding stream for affordable construction.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a Housing Trust Fund and credits to it all revenue raised by the new limits on mortgage interest, property tax, and inherited-property tax benefits, dedicated solely to affordable housing grants [S2].

Under the housing costs assistance program, an eligible family receives help equal to the difference between the fair market rent for an appropriately sized unit and the lesser of 30 percent of the family's adjusted income or 5 percent of its gross income [S3].

The housing supply assistance program funds acquisition, construction, reconstruction, and rehabilitation of affordable housing that must remain affordable for its entire useful life, with units reserved in proportion to need among extremely low-, very low-, and low-income families [S3].

Grants are distributed by formula to entitlement communities, states, and Indian tribes based on counts of families with housing problems and families paying more than 50 percent of income for housing, with minimum allotments so small jurisdictions are not left out [S3].

The bill requires citizen participation, public hearings, housing quality standards, relocation protections against displacement, and a governing board for each local administering agency that must include a formerly homeless person and low-income housing advocates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households with modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 would pay more tax: their mortgage interest and property tax deductions would shrink by 3 percentage points for every $1,000 of income over the threshold, down to a floor of 50 percent of the deduction. Heirs to inherited property would pay a gradually phased-in capital gains tax on gains that accrued before the inheritance, under the repeal of the stepped-up basis rule.

drawbacks.text: The threshold of $75,000 in adjusted gross income in 1995 dollars reached well beyond the very wealthy, so the deduction phase-down would have raised housing-related taxes on many upper-middle-income homeowners, and it would apply automatically to years beginning after 1995 [S3].

Repealing the stepped-up basis rule and treating inherited property as a gift would impose significant record-keeping burdens on families and estates, since heirs would need to establish the original cost basis of assets acquired decades earlier [S3].

The rental assistance payments go to the owners and mortgage servicers of the units families occupy, and the supply program explicitly allows for-profit housing providers to receive assistance, so a meaningful share of the new spending would flow to landlords and developers [S3].

The bill phases in the deduction limits and the tax on inherited gains gradually (deduction floor of 50 percent reached by 2000; tax on inherited gains reaching 25 percent of gain in 1999), meaning the trust fund would start small and grow over years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a large, dedicated stream of rental aid and permanently affordable housing for low-income families, paid for by narrowing tax preferences that mostly benefit households above $75,000 and people inheriting appreciated assets. The strongest honest objection is that the $75,000 threshold and the carryover-basis change would have hit some upper-middle-income families and created real tax complexity, and that some money would flow to landlords and for-profit developers rather than directly to families. The bill was never drafted into a hearing or mark-up, so none of these design questions were ever tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to Ways and Means and Banking and Financial Services in February 1995, sent to the Housing and Community Opportunity subcommittee in March, and no hearing, mark-up, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the Federal Housing Trust Fund Act of 1995 on February 22, 1995, joined by four Democratic cosponsors [S1].

The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Banking and Financial Services Committee, splitting jurisdiction because the bill both raises tax revenue and creates a housing program [S5].
On March 10, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity; that was the final action in its entire history [S5].
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, without ever receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above $75,000 kept their full mortgage interest and property tax deductions, and heirs kept the ability to inherit appreciated property without paying capital gains tax on gains accrued before the inheritance. No one gained affordable housing, because the fund was never created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Higher-income homeowners and heirs to inherited assets

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all five sponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored, but the absence of any floor action means the partisan shape of the full chamber was never tested.

industries.note: Their mortgage interest and property tax deductions would be phased down to as low as 50 percent, raising their federal taxes to fund housing aid for low-income families.

industries.industry: Heirs and estates of inherited wealth
industries.note: Repealing the stepped-up basis rule would expose inherited gains to a gradually phased-in capital gains tax, ending a major intergenerational wealth transfer benefit.

Assistance payments would flow to owners of units occupied by assisted families under multi-year contracts, giving landlords a reliable public payment stream, though units must meet housing quality standards.

The supply program funds acquisition, construction, and rehabilitation and explicitly allows for-profit providers, creating new subsidized work — but financed units must stay affordable for their entire useful life.
